newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Report warns of chemical weapons threat in Balkans.
newsitem.headline: Report warns of chemical weapons threat in Balkans.

text.p: The presence of chemical weapons in former Yugoslavia poses a potential threat to peace and arms control efforts in the Balkans, a human rights watchdog agency said on Friday.

Republics in the former Yugoslavia are all capable of producing chemical weapons and Serbia in particular maintains a sophisticated chemical weapons programme, a report issued by Human Rights Watch said.

The agency said stockpiles and production of chemical weapons could trigger a regional arms race unless the international community applies pressure on Balkan states to abandon production and destroy chemical agents they possess.

Human Rights Watch, a private U.S.-based agency monitoring human rights and arms control, accused the international community and the United States in particular of turning a blind eye to the danger of chemical weapons in the region.

The report said Washington, as main sponsor of the peace treaty that ended the Yugoslav conflict, "has a special responsibility to make public the information it has on the chemical weapons production capabilities that exist in the former Yugoslavia...".
The report alleged that the Moslem-led Bosnian government army produced crude chemical munitions during the 1992-95 war which followed Bosnia's secession from Serbian-dominated Yugoslavia.
Serb, Croat and Moslem armies are believed to have used non-lethal chemical irritants such as tear gas during the Bosnian war, the report said, quoting from U.S. military documents.
Rival armies repeatedly accused each other of employing of more dangerous chemicals but Human Rights Watch said those allegations have yet to be confirmed.
Citing interviews with former employees of the Yugoslav army, the report said that Serbia had inherited much of the extensive chemical weapons programme developed by the military in old Yugoslavia.
Before the war, the Yugoslav army produced weapons using the nerve agent sarin, the blister agent sulfur mustard, the hallucinatory agent BZ and non-lethal irritants, the report said.
Human Rights Watch said there were strong indications that Serbia and Montenegro, which now comprise Yugoslavia, continues to maintain the chemical weapons programme.

The report said that the future use of chemical weaponry in the Balkans "cannot be discounted", partly because the Serbs no longer enjoyed unsurpassed military superiority as they did during much of the Bosnian conflict.
